overview: When the federal government pays for disaster recovery, states, tribes and territories also get money to cover "management costs," the administrative work of running recovery projects. This bill lets them keep any management-cost money left over when a grant is closed out, instead of losing it. They could then use those leftover funds within five years to build their ability to prepare for, recover from, or reduce the impact of future disasters, or to cover management costs for other disasters and prevention projects. The change applies only to disasters declared, and funded, after the bill becomes law, and it does not authorize any new spending. It also asks the Government Accountability Office, Congress's watchdog agency, to study whether the amounts set aside for management costs are appropriate. As of October 3, 2025, the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee had reported it to the full House.
for: Supporters say letting governments keep unspent administrative money gives them a reason to finish and close out recovery projects faster and helps them build up staff and planning for the next disaster.
against: Critics say money left over from one disaster could instead be returned to the federal disaster fund, and broad uses for leftover funds could make it harder to track how disaster dollars are spent.
